Venture facts: the firm notes primary venture partners insights and harlem capital vc insights (press and transcripts), plus wss private markets wealth. Nothing here is a judgment on which plan was right. A plan can be sound and unlucky. This file resolves the forecasts and shows what each plan ran into.

How fast it turned. - The 10y−2y curve inverted on July 6, 2022, four trading days after the decision date. - The first SLOOS reading after the decision jumped from easing to +24% net tightening, and it stayed above 30% for five straight quarters. - The fed funds rate went from 1.21% to 5.33% in twelve months.

How it ended. There was no Shock. Lending standards normalized in 2024 while the Fed held at 5.33%, a soft landing. The scenario map reads this as non-bank lenders filling the gap the banks left (wss scenario map, data finding 3).

The lesson about the dashboard. On the decision date every lagging gauge said Boom. Public stress gauges went on to read calm through most of the drought (VIX at 15–16 in 2023Q2–Q4). Only the bank channel stayed lit. A plan that waited for public confirmation would have waited through the whole drought.

Resolving your forecasts

# Forecast Resolution
1 Regime in 2023Q2 C Drought (bank channel). Score 1 if you said Drought.
2 SLOOS > 30% in some 2023 quarter Yes. All four quarters: 44.8, 46.0, 50.8, 33.9.
3 Fund II first close ≥ X% of target by your date Score against the evidence below. If your date was before 2024 and your plan was Hold (launch mid-2023), the evidence says the odds were poor for an emerging manager.

Calibration score. For forecasts 1 and 2, compute |p − outcome|, where outcome is 1 if it happened and 0 if not. Log both in JUDGMENT-LEDGER.md. For forecast 3, write one sentence on whether the evidence supports your number.

What real seed managers ran into (the evidence for forecast 3)

  • The scaled manager ran for the window, and made it. Primary closed $425M in September 2022 ($275M Fund IV plus a $150M Select opportunity fund), one quarter into the turn. That is plan 3 executed by a firm with institutional LPs and a brand. It went on to raise $625M for Fund V in February 2026, after the drought. (primary venture partners insights.)
  • The emerging manager raised before the turn, then met it on the next fund. Harlem closed Fund II ($134M) in 2021, at the top. Its Fund III, targeting $150M, appears in an SEC filing in 2024, and the sources found no announced close. It raised into the post-drought LP squeeze plus a backlash against diversity-focused funds. (harlem capital vc insights and press.)
  • Why LPs froze. Fund distributions fell to post-GFC lows relative to NAV, and the denominator effect pushed institutions to pause new commitments. Seed managers also sat behind multi-stage firms in LP budgets. (wss private markets wealth §6; primary venture partners insights §8.)
  • The peer's call. The mid-2022 prediction that seed would reprice within about six months fits the regime turn that followed. No transcript gives a dated seed-valuation series, so this is directionally confirmed, not measured.

What each plan ran into

Plan Market it met What went right What went wrong
1. Hold Fund II launch in mid-2023 landed in the middle of the drought Fund I kept deploying through 2022–23 at reset prices, the strongest entry window in the cycle The mid-2023 raise met LPs with no distributions and full allocations. This is the fund-timing risk in apply wss to venture Concept 9.
2. Brace Same raise problem; Fund I slowed into the best prices Reserves defended winners through the A-round squeeze; no portfolio was forced into a down round Slowing deployment during a drought buys at the bottom less, the opposite of Law 3's prize. And the raise problem wasn't solved.
3. Run for the window Q3 2022 launch, one quarter before the Drought quarters Primary shows it could work for a manager LPs already knew For a $150M emerging manager, a smaller-target raise in Q3 2022 meant pitching LPs who were already watching the denominator. The plan works only if you can close in a quarter or two.

The pattern the data supports: the decision was really about the raise, not the pace. Deployment through the drought was the opportunity. Fundraising through it was the threat. The plans that separated those two did best. For example, run for the window and keep deploying Fund I at pace, with an LP-approved extension as the backstop.

Red-team prompts for your memo

  • Did you name the bank channel (or any leading indicator) as the one to trust, or did you reason from VIX and spreads?
  • Did you use a base rate? Both times since 1990 that a Boom gave way to high rates (2005, 2022), a Drought followed: about three years later in 2007Q4, and immediately in 2022Q4 (wss scenario map, data finding 2). That is n = 2, a thin base rate, so a calibrated memo should say so rather than treat it as a law.
  • Did your fatal risk name the LP side (distributions, the denominator effect), or only the portfolio side?
  • Meta-question: which note, had you read it, would have changed the memo? Likely candidates: canon tetlock superforecasting (base rates) or wss private markets wealth §6 (the distribution clock).
